accroche: The guards did not turn cruel on their own. The archives show they had been told to be.
contenu_vulgarise:
August 1971, in the basement of the Stanford psychology department. Twenty-four students chosen by lot: some guards, the others prisoners. The experiment was supposed to last two weeks; it is stopped after six days. The guards became brutal, the prisoners broke down.

The conclusion went around the world: put anyone in a uniform and a situation, and they will take on the role. The study became one of the most cited in the discipline, and one of the pillars of the idea that the situation outweighs the person.

## What the Archives Say

In 2019, the French researcher Thibault Le Texier publishes in *American Psychologist* the result of a methodical going-through of the experiment's archives, kept at Stanford: recordings, session notes, correspondence.

The picture changes completely.

The guards did not slide spontaneously into cruelty. They had received precise instructions on how to treat the prisoners, and were encouraged when they were harsh. They were, moreover, not treated as experimental subjects, but as research assistants associated with the project. Several participants said afterward that they had never got caught up in it, and had simply played the role expected of them.

The experiment therefore does not demonstrate what it is made to say. It does not show that the situation transforms people: it shows that people do what they are asked, when they are asked explicitly and then congratulated.

## Why It Held for Fifty Years

The study has never been reproduced under these conditions. Zimbardo had circulated the results by press release from the second day of the experiment, in August 1971, before any academic publication. It then circulated through the book, the documentary, and the school textbook. It told an irresistible story: any one of us, in the right setting.

Zimbardo has contested these conclusions, and the discussion has continued in the journals. Several textbooks have since removed the experiment from their chapters on the power of situations, or present it only as a case from the history of science.

## What This Shifts

There remains a question more uncomfortable than the experiment itself: why did such a fragile result become common knowledge, taught for half a century?

The answer probably lies in what the thesis relieved us of. If the situation does everything, no one is truly responsible for anything. That is precisely what the archives no longer allow us to say, and perhaps that is why they had not been opened.

repere.texte: The guards had received precise instructions on how to treat the prisoners, and were not treated as experimental subjects but as research assistants.
repere.source: Thibault Le Texier, “Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment,” American Psychologist, 2019

carte.punch: The Stanford guards did not turn cruel. They had been told to be.
carte.idee: In 2019, Thibault Le Texier goes through the archives: precise instructions given to the guards, encouragement when they got tougher, participants who say they never got caught up in it. The experiment does not show what it has been made to say for fifty years.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Le Texier (2019) — Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The article that tipped the experiment's status.

quiz.question: What did the archives of the Stanford experiment, gone through in 2019, reveal?
choix: That the prisoners had been recruited from among former inmates
That the experiment had in fact lasted the planned two weeks
That the guards had received explicit instructions to be harsh
That the results had been made up out of whole cloth
quiz.explication: The guards did not transform spontaneously: they were instructed, encouraged, and regarded as research assistants rather than as subjects. The raw facts, the lot drawing, the stop on the sixth day, are not disputed; it is their interpretation that collapses, since the situation alone does not explain the behaviors observed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many students are chosen by lot for the Stanford experiment, and in what roles?
choix: Twelve students, divided into guards and prisoners
Twenty-four students, divided into guards and prisoners
Twenty-four students, all prisoners under the watch of professionals
Fifty students, divided into three groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Twenty-four students are chosen by lot in August 1971: some guards, the others prisoners, for an experiment planned for two weeks and stopped on the sixth day.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How were the guards actually regarded by the researchers, according to the archives?
choix: As anonymous subjects unaware of the purpose of the study
As paid actors recruited from a local troupe
As volunteers recruited with no prior information
As research assistants associated with the project
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The archives show that the guards were not treated as experimental subjects, but as research assistants associated with the project, and were encouraged when they were harsh.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Zimbardo make the first results of the experiment public?
choix: By a press release from the second day of the experiment
Only after peer review of the 2019 article
By an article published as early as 1971, before the end of the experiment
At a press conference held a year after the experiment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Zimbardo circulates the results by press release from the second day of the experiment, in August 1971, well before any academic publication on the subject.
